newsitem.title: USA: Smoke trial defense unlikely to start until September - judge.
newsitem.headline: Smoke trial defense unlikely to start until September - judge.

text.p: Tobacco companies fighting a $5 billion secondhand-smoke lawsuit are unlikely to start their defense before Sept. 2, the trial judge said on Friday.

Already well into its third month, the landmark trial has been dominated by jury selection and testimony by scientists, physicians, engineers and two former U.S. surgeon generals supporting the claims against the U.S. tobacco industry by an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants allegedly sickened by passengers smoking aboard U.S. airliners.
Attorneys for the tobacco companies told Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye that their defense would take three weeks, or 10 to 15 court days, at most.

Susan Rosenblatt, an attorney for the flight attendants, estimated that the plaintiffs would continue presenting evidence through next week and would likely rest their case on Aug. 25. The balance of that week will be devoted to lawyers arguments over which documents and other evidence will be given to the six jurors who will decide the case, Kaye said.
"We're smack up against October," Kaye said.
The flight attendants claim in their lawsuit that seven tobacco companies and two trade groups sold cigarettes while knowing their health risks and conspiring to keep that information from Americans.

The tobacco companies deny the conspiracy charges and say the incidence of lung cancer, emphysema and other tobacco-related disorders among the flight attendants was no higher than that of other people.
